big_idea: Pattern rules also work with numbers — we can build repeating number parades up to 50 and explain the rule.
learning_intention: We are learning to use pattern rules with whole numbers up to 50, build a number parade, and explain its rule.
student_learning_goal: I can build a repeating number parade up to 50, name its rule, and lead it.
success_criteria: I can use the rule from an animal parade to build a number parade up to 50.
I can write at least 6 numbers in my parade strip in the correct order.
I can lead my partner through my parade and explain the rule out loud.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from previous lessons (PATTERN, CORE, RULE, MISSING, EXTEND, JUSTIFY all up)
One pre-built animal AAB parade for the opening reveal: Bea-Bea-Finn-Bea-Bea-Finn
One matching pre-built number parade with the same AAB rule using the numbers 2 and 5: 2-2-5-2-2-5-2-2-5
Hundred chart or number line (0–50) posted on the math wall — every child can see it
Dry-erase markers (one per pair) for writing numbers in laminated parade strips
Summative worksheet 'Lead the Number Parade' (one per child)
Summative rubric (one per child OR one class clipboard with student-name rows pre-filled)
Junior Pattern Conductor certificates printed and ready for the closing ceremony — keep hidden until the ceremony
Optional: small paper crowns or 'Conductor' name tags for the leading phase

minds_on.hook: Coco wants to know — can pattern rules work with NUMBERS too? Today we will find out, and then YOU lead the parade.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Coco. Beside him, lay the animal AAB strip and, parallel below it, the number AAB strip (2-2-5).

Say to students: 'All week we have parades with animals, sounds, bodies. Today Coco asks: can we make a parade with NUMBERS? Look — here is the animal parade: Bea-Bea-Finn-Bea-Bea-Finn. What is the rule?' (AAB.) 'Yes! Now look at the number parade right below it: 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 5. Where is A and where is B?' Take responses. (A is 2, B is 5.) 'Same rule! AAB. We just translated animals into numbers.'

Point to the hundred chart. 'Numbers can be small like 2, or bigger — up to 50 today. The rule does not care HOW big the numbers are, only the ORDER and how they REPEAT.' Quick demo: build a number parade using 10 and 25. 'A is 10, B is 25. AAB rule means: 10, 10, 25, 10, 10, 25. Read it with me.' Class reads.

'Today YOU are the Conductor. You pick a rule. You pick numbers. You build a parade up to 50. You lead it. By end of class, every one of you is a Junior Pattern Conductor.' Smile. Hold up a hidden corner of one certificate.
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet, facing the two parallel parade strips.
Read the animal parade and name its rule (AAB).
Read the number parade and identify A and B.
Watch the teacher build a fresh number parade with bigger numbers (10 and 25).

steps.instruction: Phase 1 — PLAN (5 min). Hand out the summative worksheet. Each child works independently at their desk. They pick a rule (AB, ABB, AAB, or ABC) and write it in the 'My Rule' box at the top. They draw or write the CORE in the 'My Core' box (a small loop showing the repeating part — e.g., for AAB, draw two animal silhouettes and one different).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Conductors — first you PLAN. In the My Rule box write the letters of your rule. In the My Core box draw or write the part that will repeat. Be sure your rule and your core match. Take 5 minutes.'

steps.instruction: Phase 2 — BUILD an animal parade (8 min). Children draw or sticker their animal parade across an 8-cell strip on the worksheet, repeating their core. They must extend forward enough to fill all 8 cells. Then they LOOP the core (draw an oval around the first repetition).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now BUILD. Use your rule to fill all 8 cells with animals. Loop the FIRST core — the part that starts to repeat. Read your parade quietly to yourself to check.' Begin one-on-one rubric conferences during this phase — ask each child to read their parade aloud and ask 'what would cell 9 be?'

steps.instruction: Phase 3 — TRANSLATE to a number parade (8 min). Below the animal parade, an empty 8-cell strip. Children pick TWO numbers between 1 and 50 (one for A, one for B; for ABC rules, three numbers). They write the two-or-three chosen numbers in a small KEY box, then fill the 8-cell strip with numbers using the SAME rule as the animal parade above. Hundred chart available for reference — copying numbers is fine.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now TRANSLATE. Pick TWO numbers between 1 and 50 — your choice. Write A = ___ and B = ___ in the key. Then fill the number strip with the SAME rule as your animals. Look at the hundred chart if you need help writing a number.' Continue rubric conferences. By end of Phase 3 most children should be scored on at least 3 of 4 expectations.

steps.instruction: Phase 4 — LEAD (7 min). Children pair up on the carpet. Partner A reads their parade aloud (animal first, then number). Partner B has to: (1) name the rule, (2) predict cell 9 of both parades, and (3) say one thing they noticed. Then swap. Use this phase to confirm uncertain rubric scores and upgrade where Level 4 thinking shows up.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now LEAD. Find a partner on the carpet. Conductor A — read your animal parade, then your number parade, out loud. Conductor B — name the rule, predict cell 9, and say one thing you notice. Swap. Both conductors get to lead.'

steps.instruction: Phase 5 — REVISE & REFLECT (8 min). Children return to their desk with their summative worksheet. Teacher prompts: 'You just heard your animal parade and number parade out loud, and you led a partner through both. Look at your worksheet now. Did your partner stop you anywhere? Did your number parade rule actually match your animal parade rule? Find ONE thing on your worksheet to fix — pencil it in.' Each child must REVISE at least one element. Then they draw a small star next to the strongest part of their parade and a question mark next to the trickiest part — these become the consolidation seeds and the formative evidence for the rubric. The teacher walks the room with the summative rubric clipboard, looking specifically for whether children can self-identify an animal/number mismatch (the most common error) without prompting.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two final jobs, Pattern Conductors. First — you heard your parade out loud and led a friend. Be your own teacher now. Find ONE thing to revise on your worksheet and fix it. Pattern Conductors always check their own work, especially when translating between animals and numbers. Then — draw a star next to the part you're PROUDEST of and a question mark next to the part that was HARDEST. We share these in our circle.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Provide a pre-printed AB rule on the worksheet so the child only chooses the elements (animals + numbers). Provide a number bank of small numbers (1, 2, 5, 10, 20) so the child does not have to invent. Pair with a confident peer for the lead phase.
differentiation.for_extending: Challenge the child to use an ABC rule with three different animals AND three different numbers, including at least one number greater than 30. Stretch question during the conference: 'If your parade had 30 cells, who would be in cell 30? What number would be there?' This previews Grade 2 number-pattern reasoning.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a worksheet with the animal cells pre-numbered 1–8 below them so the child can visually align the rule. Provide a sentence frame for the lead phase: 'My rule is ___. My numbers are ___ and ___.' Accept gestures and pointing as part of the lead.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After completing the worksheet, the pair stands and PARADE-WALKS the rule, calling animal names on the steps. Then walks again calling the numbers. Walking ties the abstract rule to physical rhythm and seals retention.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: SUMMATIVE evidence. Look at the worksheet artifact and the partner-lead conversation. For each child: did they pick a valid rule, build it correctly, translate to numbers preserving the rule, and explain the rule aloud during the lead? Score against the 4-level rubric (see assessment_suite).
formative_check.how_to_record: Score each child on the summative rubric (4 levels × 4 expectations) using the worksheet as primary evidence and the partner-lead conversation as confirming evidence.

discussion_prompts: Who would like to lead the WHOLE class through their parade? (Take 2–3 children. They read their animal parade, then their number parade, while the class chants the rule.)
What was the trickiest part of making a NUMBER parade compared to an animal parade? Why?
What was your favourite parade you built this week — across all 5 days — and what was its rule?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child receives a Junior Pattern Conductor certificate (the teacher reads it briefly at the front and hands it over with a high five). Each child then leaves the carpet calling out their rule one last time as their parade name ('I am Conductor ___, and my rule is ___').

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Completed 'Lead the Number Parade' summative worksheet plus partner-lead conversation observations. Scored against the 4-level rubric covering all four expectations (C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4). Plus end-of-unit reflection sheet completed alongside the certificate ceremony.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: This is the unit's summative moment. The four-phase task (Plan-Build-Translate-Lead) is designed so the worksheet artifact alone gives evidence on C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, and C1.4. The partner-lead conversation upgrades children to Level 4 when they can independently explain why the rule works — including the new C1.4 layer of relating animals to numbers up to 50.

expanded_walkthrough.title: The Number Parade Reveal — Translating to Numbers
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: C1.4 is the unique Grade 1 expectation: using repeating patterns to describe relationships among whole numbers up to 50. Children have practiced animal, sound, and body translations all week. Numbers are the abstract leap. The reveal needs to make explicit that the rule does not change when the things change, even when the things are numbers. Without this anchoring, children may treat the number parade as a counting exercise rather than a pattern exercise.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Two parallel parade strips on the carpet, both showing the AAB rule: Strip 1 = Bea-Bea-Finn-Bea-Bea-Finn animal version, Strip 2 = 2-2-5-2-2-5 number version (numbers written large on cards or directly on a laminated strip). A Core Loop Frame ready. The hundred chart visible on the math wall. Coco the puppet visible. Anchor chart with PATTERN, CORE, RULE, JUSTIFY all up.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Hold up Coco. Say to students: 'All week our parades had animals, sounds, bodies. Coco's last question for the week is the biggest one — can a parade be made of NUMBERS?'

Point to Strip 1 (animals). 'Read this parade with me.' Lead the class: 'Bea, Bea, Finn, Bea, Bea, Finn.' Place the loop around the first Bea-Bea-Finn group. 'Core?' (Bea-Bea-Finn.) 'Rule?' (AAB.) Confirm.

Now point to Strip 2 (numbers, parallel below). 'Now this parade. Read with me.' Lead: '2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 5.' Place the loop around the first 2-2-5 group. 'Core?' (2-2-5.) 'Rule?' Wait. The class should land on AAB. Validate. 'Same rule. Two parades, same rule.'

Pause. Step back. 'A is the bear. A is also the 2. They are not the same THING — but they play the same ROLE in the rule. B is the fox. B is also the 5. Same role.'

Pick up a fresh card. 'I want to show you something powerful. Let's change A. A is now 10. B is now 25. Same AAB rule. What does the parade look like?' Take responses. Build it: 10, 10, 25, 10, 10, 25. 'Read it.' Class reads. 'And the rule is still…?' (AAB.)

Final stretch — point to the hundred chart. 'Today on your worksheet you can pick any two numbers from this chart, anywhere up to 50, and use them as A and B. The rule does the work. The rule does not care if A is 2 or 47. The rule just says: A, A, B, A, A, B. You are the Conductor. You pick the numbers. You build the parade.'
expected_student_responses: Many children will recognize the AAB rule instantly in the number parade after a week of practice.
Some children will get confused by the SIZE of the numbers (e.g., asking 'is 50 too big?'). Reassure: any number on the chart is fine.

A child may try to make a COUNTING pattern (1, 2, 3, 4) instead of a REPEATING pattern. This is a category mistake — counting up is a growing pattern (Grade 2). Redirect: 'Today we are doing REPEATING. Pick two numbers and let them repeat.'

A child may pick the same number for A and B (e.g., A = 5, B = 5). Validate the math instinct, then redirect: 'If A and B are the same, the parade is just one number over and over — that's fine, but it does not show the rule. Pick two DIFFERENT numbers so the rule shines.'
A child may invent an interesting twist (e.g., A = 10, B = 20, an ABBA rule). Celebrate and let them write it on the worksheet as a stretch.
common_misconceptions: Confusing repeating patterns with counting patterns — a child writes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 in the number strip thinking they have made a pattern. Counting up is a growing pattern (Grade 2 territory).
Treating the size of the number as part of the rule — 'this is an AAB rule with small numbers and that is an AAB rule with big numbers, so they are different rules'. They are the same rule.
Picking two numbers but not using them in AAB order — placing them randomly. Loop the core to redirect.
Stopping at 6 cells because the animal parade was 6 cells, even though the worksheet has 8.
recovery_moves: If a child writes a counting pattern: have them point to the rule on their own worksheet ('Your rule is AAB. Where is the A? Where is the B? In a counting pattern, every cell is different — that's not your rule.'). Then start over with the worksheet's number bank.

If a child treats number size as part of the rule: build two AAB parades side by side, one with (1, 2) and one with (40, 50). Read both. Ask 'what is the rule of each?' (AAB both.) 'See — same rule. Size does not matter.'

If a child places numbers randomly: hand them the loop and say 'show me the core'. They cannot. Ask them to write A under each cell where A goes and B under each cell where B goes — first. Then write the numbers.
If a child stops short of 8 cells: 'Your worksheet wants 8 cells. Use the rule to fill the rest. What is cell 7? What is cell 8?'

worksheet_brief.purpose: Summative performance task for the full unit (C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4). Each child plans a rule, builds an animal parade, translates it to a number parade using whole numbers up to 50, and leads a partner through it.

parts_outline.task: Top-of-page header: a 'My Rule' box (2in wide, ~1in tall, child writes the rule label e.g., AAB), a 'My Core' box (3in wide, ~1.5in tall, child draws a small loop containing the core animals), and a small reference legend showing the four animals.
An 8-cell parade strip labelled 'My Animal Parade'. Student fills all 8 cells with their animal parade following the rule from Part 1. They then loop the FIRST core (the part that starts to repeat).

A 'My Number Key' box showing 'A = ___' and 'B = ___' (and 'C = ___' if the rule needs it). Child picks numbers between 1 and 50 and writes them. Below: an empty 8-cell parade strip labelled 'My Number Parade'. Student writes the numbers in all 8 cells using the SAME rule as Part 2. Bottom of page: a small writing line 'My rule works because ___' for the justify-aloud sentence to be written or scribed.
